tool_result_content:
# Setting Up TypeScript

The page describes three installation routes, depending on how you plan to use TypeScript.

## Per-project installation (recommended)

The page recommends a per-project install so each project can use its own TypeScript version and stay consistent.

**Via npm** (requires [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/)):

```bash
npm install typescript --save-dev
```

You can also use yarn or pnpm. All three support lockfiles, so everyone on a team uses the same version. Then run the compiler with:

```bash
npx tsc
```

**Via Visual Studio / NuGet** (for MSBuild projects such as ASP.NET Core):

- Use the **Manage NuGet Packages** window (right-click a project node), or
- Run this in **Tools > NuGet Package Manager > Package Manager Console**:

```powershell
Install-Package Microsoft.TypeScript.MSBuild
```

For project types that don't support NuGet, install the [TypeScript Visual Studio extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=TypeScriptTeam.typescript-593) via **Extensions > Manage Extensions**.

## Global installation

A global install makes `tsc` available in any terminal, which is useful for one-off experiments. The page advises against it for real codebases because it hurts reproducible builds across machines.

```bash
npm install -g typescript
```

The page says this installs the latest version, currently **7.0**. A 7.1 beta is also announced.

## Using TypeScript-compatible transpilers

Tools like these convert TypeScript to JavaScript faster or fit existing build pipelines, but they don't perform type-checking. You still need the `typescript` package, and you should enable [`isolatedModules`](/tsconfig/#isolatedModules) in your tsconfig.

- **Babel**: via `@babel/plugin-transform-typescript`
- **swc**: a Rust-based transpiler
- **Sucrase**: a Babel fork focused on development-mode speed, with native TypeScript support
